transcript.speaker: gm
transcript.text:
The low sun lays the church tower’s shadow across Harrowby Green, between two crowds holding their ground: villagers with hayforks and rakes by the well; mud-caked refugees among nine carts, two cows, and geese that have declined to respect the occasion. In the middle, a small girl sits cross-legged in a ring of chalk and salt, arms folded and chin up. A thin young woman in a green University gown stands over her, a straw doll tied at her belt and grey ash on her thumb. Nearby, a stooped old man pleads; a big lad with an eel-spear shouts about goblins.

The young woman spots you. Relief crosses her face before duty catches up. “A stranger. Good. You’ll serve as the stranger’s eye required by the Statutes at a ward-judgment. Please come here.” The whole green turns to look at you. What do you do?

transcript.speaker: player
transcript.text: I stride into the middle of the green, hop up onto the lip of the well so everyone can see me, and raise one hand. "Friends! Neighbours! Geese! I accept the honour of stranger's eye. But a matter this grave cannot be settled by shouting. I call this green to order as a Public Meeting. Point of order, all hayforks to be held prongs-down while the meeting is in session." I turn to the young woman in the gown. "Madam, what is the question before the assembly?"

transcript.speaker: gm
transcript.text:
The hayforks tilt prongs-down with varying degrees of obedience. One goose also lowers its head, though it appears to be considering the matter personally. The crowd quiets enough to hear.

Hester squares her shoulders. “The question is whether Pip Callow, who took the corn mother from the bounds-stone, makes amends before the parish—or receives the thief’s mark, as the Statutes require. The mark lasts a year and a day. The way out is hers to take.”

Oswin bows his head. “Friend, spare the child, if you can. And spare my people the road tonight. One more week on the green is all we ask.”

Ned grips his eel-spear. “The goblins took our seed-grain. Burnt mill, north up the river path. Come with us tonight—we can get it back. That’s the real trouble here.”

Pip looks up at you. “I’m not sorry. Are you actually a stranger, or just dressed like one?” Hester waits, thumb grey with ash. What do you do?

transcript.speaker: player
transcript.text: I bow to Pip from atop the well. "Madam, I am a stranger to Harrowby, but no stranger to procedure." I turn back to the crowd. "Under the Ancient Right of Reply, which as every schoolchild knows dates back to the Great Turnip Parliament of the year of the Long Frost, the accused may address the meeting before any mark is given. Show of hands! All in favour of hearing the child speak?" I raise my own hand high and count loudly. Then, to Pip, gently: "The floor is yours. Why did you take the corn mother?"

transcript.speaker: gm
transcript.text:
A few hands go up. Yours is the first; then Oswin’s, and several villagers follow, some looking relieved to have been given a task that doesn’t involve a weapon. A hayfork stays prongs-down. The geese abstain.

Hester’s mouth tightens, but she gives a small, formal nod. “The accused may speak. That is fair procedure, whether or not the Great Turnip Parliament existed.”

Pip uncurls one arm. “I took it because if there was no corn mother, there’d be no ward. Then nobody could make us leave.” Her eyes flick to Oswin, then back to you. “I was going to put it back. I’m not sorry they need it.”

Oswin’s brass-topped staff creaks in his grip. Ned goes quiet, watching his sister. Hester waits for Pip to say more—or for you to ask.

transcript.speaker: player
transcript.text: I nod gravely, as if Pip has just delivered the finest speech since the Turnip Parliament. "Thank you. The meeting notes the accused acted out of concern for her community." I turn to Hester. "Point of information, Madam Warden. Why would the ward make these people leave? What does the ward actually do, and what has the Centennial Assembly got to do with it?" Before she can answer I raise a finger. "And I hereby form a Select Committee on Wards, Dolls and Related Matters. Myself as chair, Pip Callow as recording secretary, and that goose" - I point at the goose who lowered its head earlier - "as sergeant-at-arms. Committee is quorate."

transcript.speaker: gm
transcript.text:
The goose honks at your appointment and steps onto the well’s rim. No one challenges its credentials.

Hester glances at the setting sun, then at her grey thumb. “The ward is raised at sundown on ward-night. I walk the parish bounds with the corn mother, then set it in the niche of the bounds-stone. It turns out anyone inside the bounds who isn’t of Harrowby—goblins included. They remember urgent business elsewhere and cannot settle here until spring sowing.” Her gaze passes over the carts. “The Sedgeford folk are not of the parish.”

She keeps her voice precise. “The Centennial Assembly is why Master Warden Applegarth is away. On ward-night, I speak for Harrowby.”

Oswin inclines his head. “We were given the green for two days, friend. We knew the understanding. We hoped the water might go down before it came to this.”

Ned rests his spear in the turf. “The goblins took our seed-grain. I tracked them north to the burnt mill. Five of them. Small. Scared, maybe—but they’ve got next spring’s planting.”

Pip examines the goose. “Does it get a vote?”

Hester looks again toward the church tower. The sun is level with its edge. “The committee may take its evidence. It may not postpone sundown.”

transcript.speaker: player
transcript.text: "The sergeant-at-arms has a casting vote in the event of a tie, and may bite anyone out of order," I tell Pip solemnly. Then I spread my arms to the whole green. "Then the solution is plain! If the ward turns out anyone not of Harrowby, we must make them of Harrowby. Madam Warden, do the Statutes say how a person becomes of the parish? I put a motion to this Public Meeting: that the people of Sedgeford be admitted as parishioners of Harrowby, here, tonight, before the sun goes down. Villagers of Harrowby, this is your green and your vote. All in favour, raise your rakes!"

transcript.speaker: gm
transcript.text:
The rakes rise in a scattered wave: some villagers lift them at once, others follow after looking around to see whether this is a lawful sort of thing to do. Several stay down. The vote is not unanimous; the green has no agreed rule for what a raised rake means.

Hester’s ash-grey thumb presses against the corn mother at her belt. “The Statutes do not make a parish by vote. They do, however, say who the ward counts as belonging to it.” She hesitates, eyes on the sun slipping past the church tower. “A stranger who breaks Harrowby bread and salt with a parishioner at the bounds-stone is guest to the ward while it stands.”

Oswin looks up sharply. The words seem to stir an old recollection. Hester continues, too quickly: “It must be Harrowby bread. And salt. At the bounds-stone. I have not said this would be safe for thirty-one people.”

The goose honks from its perch. Hester turns to you. “Is that the committee’s motion, then?”

transcript.speaker: player
transcript.text: "The motion is amended!" I cry. "The committee moves a Great Supper of Bread and Salt at the bounds-stone, one Harrowby host for every Sedgeford guest. Pip, write that down." I turn to the villagers with my most stirring voice. "People of Harrowby! A hundred years from now, at the next Centennial, they will ask: when the floodwater came, what did Harrowby do? Did it hold up hayforks, or did it hold out a loaf? Every household, fetch bread and a pinch of salt, and choose a guest!" Then, lower, to Hester: "Madam Warden, you said it might not be safe for thirty-one people. Not safe how? The committee needs to know before it marches anyone anywhere."

transcript.speaker: gm
transcript.text:
The villagers begin to move—some toward their cottages, others hesitating over whether a motion can make them responsible for fetching bread. Oswin lifts one hand to steady his people; no one rushes off yet.

Hester’s formal composure thins. “Not unsafe because the custom harms them. The ward would hold. I’m afraid I might not hold it properly with so many more inside it.” Her thumb rubs at the ash on her skin. “Master Warden Applegarth once covered a harvest fair. I have never raised it alone.”

Oswin studies her, then says quietly, “My grandmother had a saying. ‘Bread at the bounds makes kin of strangers.’ I thought it was only a way of teaching children manners.”

Pip leans toward the goose. “Write that down.”

Hester looks from Oswin to you. “The custom is real. If Harrowby households share bread and salt with the Sedgeford folk at the bounds-stone before sundown, the ward will count them as guests while it stands.” Her voice lowers. “But the rite must be done properly—and quickly.”

transcript.speaker: player
transcript.text: I hop down from the well and lower my voice for Hester alone. "Then the committee further resolves that the Warden shall not hold it alone. Harrowby will hold it with you. That is what a parish is for." Then, back at full volume, I squint at the sinking sun. "Time is against us, and the meeting cannot be in two places at once. By the ancient Principle of the Mountain and the Prophet, if the meeting cannot go to the stone, the stone must come to the meeting! Ned, you are a big lad. Take four strong volunteers and a cart, dig up the bounds-stone and bring it here to the green, and we shall hold the Supper right here in comfort."

transcript.speaker: gm
transcript.text:
Hester’s eyes widen at your quiet words. For a heartbeat, the ash on her thumb is the only thing she seems able to see. Then she gives one sharp nod.

“Thank you,” she says, so softly the well almost keeps it. “I will ask them to stand with me.”

At your proclamation, Ned’s face brightens. “At last, a proper job.” But Oswin catches his sleeve before he can gather volunteers. “Friend, the stone is set deep. We’d lose the light before we shifted it—and a cart won’t make it lighter.”

Hester steps between Ned and the bounds-men. “The bounds-stone stays where it is. The bread and salt must be shared there, before sundown.” Villagers start toward their homes, some carrying loaves already; others look uneasy at being assigned guests. “If Harrowby households will do this,” Hester says, “I’ll raise the ward with Sedgeford counted as guests.”

The sun is nearly at the church tower’s edge. “We have time for the rite,” she says. “Not for a committee to dig up the parish.”

transcript.speaker: player
transcript.text: "The chair accepts the Warden's ruling," I say, with only a small sigh for the stone. "This meeting stands adjourned to the bounds-stone! Procession in order of precedence: sergeant-at-arms first." I gesture grandly to the goose. Then I crouch at the edge of Pip's chalk ring. "Recording secretary, the committee has a proposal for your amends. You took the corn mother from the stone. So you walk beside the Warden, carry the salt, and help her put the ward back where you took it from. Will you do that?" I glance up at Hester. "Would the Statutes call that amends, Madam Warden? And somebody find me a loaf and a host. I am a stranger here too, and I would rather not suddenly remember urgent business elsewhere."

transcript.speaker: gm
transcript.text:
The goose sets off toward the bounds-stone at a purposeful waddle. The crowd parts for it; precedent, once established, is difficult to argue with.

Hester answers your question as she steps out of the stay-ring’s reach. “Helping restore the corn mother would be a proper amends. The Statutes don’t require a particular apology.” Her shoulders ease a fraction. “If Pip agrees, I’ll accept it.”

Pip studies you, then the chalk line. “I’ll carry the salt. I’m not saying I’m sorry.” She stands, and the ring gives way beneath her step.

A Harrowby woman brings a loaf from the bakehouse, still warm in its cloth. Hester takes it, then pauses at your request. “You are the stranger’s eye, not a guest of Harrowby. For the ward to count you as one, a parishioner must share bread and salt with you at the bounds-stone too.” She looks toward the villagers. “Who will host them?”

transcript.speaker: player
transcript.text: I fall in behind the goose and call back over my shoulder as we walk. "A show of hands, please, for hosting the stranger's eye! Volunteers will be thanked in the minutes." Then a thought stops me mid-stride. "Madam Warden, a point of order. Our sergeant-at-arms is a Sedgeford goose. So are its colleagues, and those two cows. Does the ward turn out livestock? Because this committee will not stand by while its sergeant-at-arms is struck with urgent business elsewhere. I move that the goose be hosted with bread and salt like any other guest. Pip, minute that the goose is to have the crust."

transcript.speaker: gm
transcript.text:
Hands rise across the green. One baker’s wife calls, “I’ll host the stranger. Minutes or no minutes.” Another woman offers to host the goose, provided it doesn’t come into her kitchen.

Hester keeps pace toward the bounds-stone. “The ward turns out people who aren’t of the parish. Livestock aren’t people.” She gives the goose a wary glance. “I cannot promise it will distinguish a sergeant-at-arms from any other goose.”

Pip says, “It gets the crust.”

At the stone, Hester lays out the bread and salt. Oswin’s people gather close; Harrowby households step forward with their loaves. Hester looks to you. “The ward will count the Sedgeford folk as guests if parishioners share bread and salt with them here. We have time to do this properly. Will you witness the welcome?”

transcript.speaker: player
transcript.text: I take my place beside the stone, remove my hat, and speak with all the solemnity of a man opening a new bridge. "I witness it. Let the minutes record that on the eve of the Centennial, Harrowby did not count its strangers, it fed them." I nod to Pip. "Recording secretary, the salt, if you please." Then I turn to the baker's wife, break her loaf with her, take my pinch of salt, and eat it with great ceremony. "Madam, you are a credit to the parish. The chair moves a vote of thanks to the bakehouse." I watch to be sure every Sedgeford family, Oswin, Ned and Pip included, gets a host and a crust, and that the goose gets its crust as minuted.

transcript.speaker: gm
transcript.text:
Your witness and the hosts’ open hands make the custom more than a saying. One by one, Harrowby households share bread and salt with the Sedgeford families at the bounds-stone. Oswin accepts his portion with a careful bow. Ned takes his without swagger. Pip gives the salt to Hester, then helps her set the corn mother back in its niche.

The goose gets its crust. It eats it with the grave attention of an officer receiving a medal.

Hester looks over the gathered guests, then at the sun’s last bright edge. “The ward will count them as Harrowby’s guests. They may stay.” She turns to Pip. “Your amends are accepted. There will be no mark.” Pip nods once, chin still high.

Hester gathers the corn mother. “At sundown, I walk the bounds. You may witness that too, if you wish.”
